chapter: New York 1930s and New Orleans expatriates
title: New Orleans style seen as corny; meeting Shields and Parenti
summary: Kmen moved to New York in 1933-34, met Larry Shields and Tony Parenti at Sharkey's apartment.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well, specifically, getting back to what I'm supposed to be researching, I want to get some of your attitudes about early New Orleans musicians that you've heard and have some sort of impression of. You know, whether they were considered corny or good, and how you knew them and why, and just anything.

Well, at the time that I broke into the business in a professional way, generally the New Orleans musicians were, or the New Orleans style was passe. This is a time when I was kept alive by some guys who were devoted to it, you know, more or less underground. But the average working musician, at least around my area, which would be New York area, regarded that whole kind of music as corny. They called it corny. Of course, they thought of themselves as being the utmost in modernity and so forth. But then when I went to New York, the revival, perhaps the first revival, was just beginning, and this revival really coincided, or even owed in part to Goodman's success. No doubt about that. And you remember, for a brief period, they got together as much of the original Dixieland Jazz Band as they could. And at that time, I met Larry Shields. I met him through New Orleans musicians that I had met and worked with. I met him specifically. I used to see Larry Shields and meet him up in an apartment in the Landseer Apartments in New York that was either, I know Sharky lived in that apartment, and Johnny Beresdorfer was living in that apartment.
So you met the Musicians' Ball, incidentally.
Well, the other musicians from New Orleans, it was kind of a convenient hangout, and Sharky

used to cook for us occasionally, Creole. And that's where I met Shields, and then in the same group of musicians, but in another place I met quite frequently Tony Parenti. And again, at the time he was considered pretty bad, pretty corny. In fact, I jammed with him in the apartment, and that was my impression of him. But he's still going pretty strong right now, as you know. And I thought of him as an old man then. When did you move to New York? It would be 1934, even 1933 possibly, as soon as I got out of high school. Well, Goodman wasn't a big man then. No. No. I remember very well the first Goodman broadcast on the National Biscuit Company deal that they had there, and the impact that that had on musicians around me. And I remember the first Goodman record that had any real wide circulation, both upstate, because I was New York City and my home were just a few hours apart, was a record of Sometimes I'm Happy, in which Arthur Rolini played a tenor solo and Berrigan was in the band. And the King Porter Stomp at the same time. These were the two records that really made the first big impression.
